title: Ashoka's Remorse After Kalinga
text:
Around 261 BC, eight years after his coronation, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga, a kingdom on the east coast of India in what is now Odisha. It was the only major war of his reign, and he won it.

We know what he felt about it because he said so himself, in an inscription carved on rock and set up in many parts of his empire, known as Rock Edict XIII. In it Ashoka states that 150,000 people were carried away from Kalinga, 100,000 were killed, and many times that number died. He writes that he felt deep remorse, because conquering an unconquered country meant killing, death and the deportation of people, and that this weighed heavily on him. He grieved also for the good people, priests and families caught up in it.

The edict announces that the only conquest he now valued was conquest by dhamma, a moral law of compassion, honesty and respect for all. In the years that followed Ashoka issued edicts promoting tolerance between religious groups, care for the sick, wells and shade trees along roads, and restraint in killing animals. He did not launch another war of conquest.
lesson: Look honestly at the full cost of your wins, including who paid it. What you learn may change how you choose to use your power.
